div.p: Many-core architectures are promising hardware to design hard real-time systems as they are based on simpler and thus more predictable processors than multi-core systems. However, the worst-case behavior of the Network-on-Chip (NoC) for both intercore and core to external memories or peripherals communications must be established. Several NoCs targeting hard real-time systems, made of specific hardware extensions, have been designed. However, none of these extensions are currently available in commercially existing NoC-based many-core architectures, that instead rely on wormhole switching with round-robin arbitration. In this paper, we thus demonstrate three properties of such NoC-based wormhole networks to identify worst-case scenarios and reduce the pessimism when modeling flows in contentions. We then describe and evaluate an algorithm to compute Worst-Case Traversal Time (WCTT) of flows that uses these properties. In particular, our results show that the pessimism can be reduced up to 50% compared to current state-of-the-art real-time packet schedulability analysis.

div.head: I. Introduction
div.p: In distributed hard real-time systems, the Worst-Case Traversal Time (WCTT) of all the packets generated by a flow must be lower than a predetermined deadline. Such real-time packet schedulability analysis have been done for various types of networks by taking into account the type of contentions that can occur between flows. For instance, the worst-case behavior of AFDX networks has been the subject of several studies using different analysis techniques [4]. The challenge lies in the ability to define analysis techniques that have a limited complexity, in order to give results in a reasonable amount of time, and at the same time compute WCTT values that are not too pessimistic. This can be achieved by adding assumptions at various levels: from the application level down to the network level. At the network level, the key point is to state properties between flows to lower the impact of contentions, identified by the analysis, closer to the real behavior. For instance, a grouping technique was used to improve the analysis of AFDX networks by integrating the serialization effect of flows that share a same link [12]. In this work, we focus on defining network properties on the behavior of packet transmission over many-core architectures.

Many-core architectures are indeed promising hardware to support the design of hard real-time systems [20]. They are based on simpler cores, without complex hardware mechanisms, such as for instance speculative execution or advanced branch predictors, that can be found in multi-core architectures. The timing predictability of cores within many-core architectures are thus easier to analyze, as they are made free from timing anomalies [18].

The challenge is then to analyze the worst-case behavior of the underlying Network-on-chip (NoC) [2] used for both inter-core and core to external memories or peripherals communications. However, the initial motivation when designing NoCs was to increase the average case throughput, while hard real-time systems are concerned by guarantees in worst-case scenarios. NoCs can thus be used in hard real-time systems using two approaches by either: 1) analyzing the WCTTs of flows on existing many-cores or 2) by modifying the hardware so that no contentions can occur by design, leading to straightforward WCTT for flows. Several NoC have been proposed based on the second approach [13], [14], [25]. However, none of these NoCs targeting hard real-time constraints are available in commercially existing many-core architectures, such as for instance the Tilera Tile CPUs [29], the STMicroelectronics P2012/STHORM fabric [3] or the Kalray MPPA [7]. In this work, we instead focus on the first approach: analyzing the WCTTs of flows on such existing many-cores. These many-core architectures rely on wormhole switching [21] and Round-Robin Arbitration (RRA) within routers. Using wormhole switching, a packet is divided in flow control digits (flits) of fixed size and are transmitted one by one by routers. The header flit, i.e. the first flit, contains the routing information that defines the path the next flits will follow in a pipeline way. Routers have buffers of a few flits due to the area cost of memories in chips. Flits of a same packet can thus be present on different routers and credit-based mechanisms are used to control the progression of flows. Depending on whether a single or multiple Virtual Channels (VC) [5] are supported, contentions can propagate backwards on the path of flows and thus may indirectly impact other flows [15]. Multiple VCs mean that several buffers can be used for storing flits of packets. However, most existing many-cores support a few VCs, in order to separate best effort from urgent traffic. For instance, the Tilera Tile CPUs has only a single VC, while the P2012/STHORM NoC supports two VCs. The cost of supporting many VCs is indeed expensive due to the increased buffer requirements. In addition, prioritybased wormhole [19], whose WCTT of flows have been analyzed [26], cannot be implemented on these manycores as it requires distinctive priority per flow and perpriority VC. Besides, when considering only a given VC, amongst the multiple VCs, contentions still exist as the same control flow policy is used. All this calls for studying the contentions that can occur between flows that use a same VC. In this paper, we therefore focus on analyzing the WCTT of flows over wormhole-switched NoC-based manycores assuming a single VC.

To the best of our knowledge, [23] is the first work that has studied the WCTT of flows on wormhole networks, assuming a RRA policy at input port of routers. [10] showed with an illustrative example that the model used in this work is pessimistic. In a different application domain, [9] describes a method, called Recursive Calculus (RC), to compute WCTT for wormhole networks that also use a RRA. However, it does not model the pipeline way of transmitting flits as it does not target NoCs. In a previous work, we have shown, using two examples, that modeling this pipeline transmission of flits of NoCs can greatly reduce the pessimism of the WCTT of flows [1]. Our first contribution in this paper is therefore to demonstrate three properties of wormhole-switched NoC-based manycores when analyzing contentions between flows. Our second contribution is then to evaluate how these properties can be used, in an algorithm that we propose, to significantly reduce the WCTTs of flows. Our evaluation relies on a set of synthetic benchmarks as well as real use-cases. We also compare our results to the aforementioned RC method.

The remainder of this paper is as follows. Section II describes the main results for computing WCTT of flows over NoCs and wormhole-based networks. Then, section III defines the network model we consider and the notations we use throughout the paper. Three properties of wormhole switching when analyzing contentions between flows are next demonstrated and illustrated in section IV. Section V describes the main steps of our algorithm to compute the WCTT of flows. Section VI presents the results we obtained with this algorithm on a set of synthetic benchmarks and real use-cases. Finally, section VII concludes and gives some future work.

div.head: A. Real-time NoCs
div.p: Several approaches have been used to make wormholebased NoC compatible with hard real-time systems. For instance, [30] relies on physical circuit switching in order to avoid contentions to occur, at both VC and link level. The main problem is to ensure the successful reservation of these resources at a given time, as conflicts between flows can occur. To improve bandwidth utilization, virtual circuit switching relying on a Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) policy to schedule accesses to routers and links was proposed ( [13], [14]). Again, by design, no contention can therefore occur, leading to WCTT that can easily be computed. However, the static routing schedule is inefficient for providing low latency to flows having low bandwidth requirements and requires a global notion of time. Besides, network capacities are under-utilized in the average case, as schedules are computed in the worst-case. Non-blocking routers with rate control is another approach used for instance in [7]. Contentions can only occur at the link level. The rate control limits the amount of data source nodes can emit to avoid any overflow within routers. The WCTT of flows can then be computed using queuing disciplines results [31]. However, the impact at the task level of such a flow control must be considered.

div.head: B. Priority-based wormhole networks and NoCs
div.p: Real-time communication over wormhole networks were studied before NoCs were introduced and lead to the proposal of priority-based wormhole switching [19]. Using this approach, the priority of flows is mapped over the priority bits of VCs. At each router, links are assigned to VCs of the highest priority that has a flit ready to be transmitted. [15] proposes an algorithm to compute WCTT of flows over priority-based wormhole networks. It uses a dependency graph between flows to identify both the direct and indirect contentions a flow may suffer. When an indirect flow is identified, the accuracy of WCTT values is improved, as the blocking effect of indirect flows can thus be modeled to occur only when other (periodic) blocking flows are released simultaneously. [17] also distinguishes direct from indirect contentions but by utilizing a contention tree. This graph is further used to identify when parallel transmissions of flows on disjoint concurrent paths can occur, reducing the contention interferences. However, both algorithms assume that all flows that are in indirect contentions have an impact. In this work, we state the conditions to remove this pessimistic assumption, as also pointed out by [17]. Besides, when overlapped activities on links are modeled it is only at the packet level and not at the flit level, which is also pessimistic.

Priority-based wormhole was also applied in the context of NoC. [26] presents a method for computing the WCTT of flows which integrates both direct and indirect interferences of higher-priority flows. Indirect interferences are treated as additional release jitter on flows that directly interfere with the analyzed flow. [26] also shows that values obtained in [17] can be optimistic, as the worst case scenario do not occur when flows are released simultaneously. More recently, [22] analyzes WCTT of flows of applications designed following a partitioning approach but where runtime migrations are decided by the applications themselves. As paths of flows cannot be known at design time, the size of the search space of the worst-case scenario is higher. Compared to [26], a lower complexity method, but more pessimistic, is thus used. It is also assumed that flows in direct contention must also reach their destinations before the analyzed flows can progress, which is pessimistic.

div.head: C. Best-effort NoCs and recursive methods
div.p: In the context of best effort NoC, [23] extends the contention tree used in [17] to identify three basic contentions patterns. Complex contentions are then decomposed into these patterns and Network Calculus (NC) is used to compute WCTT of flows. [10] clearly showed that this leads to over-dimensioning the resources. [16] presents a recursive algorithm to compute the WCTT of flows induced by contentions on the path of the analyzed flow. In [24], its tightness is improved as the RRA is modeled and therefore only a single flow per port in contention, in the worst case the one of maximum size, can use the link before the analyzed flow.

RC [9] is a method to compute the WCTT of flows for the SpaceWire network, that also uses wormhole switch-ing. Similarly to [24] and introduced simultaneously, the method recursively analyzes the contention in the path of the analyzed flow. At each router, the direct flows are identified and their delays are computed by thus taking into account indirect flows. As a RRA is assumed, at each input port, the maximum delay from the set of flows in direct or indirect contentions is added. [11] shows that, in general, NC gives tighter WCTT values than RC. However, RC is less pessimistic than NC when the network is saturated. As in [16], [24], this method does not take advantage of the pipeline transmission of flits: packets must reach their destinations before the next one can progress. Recently, [6] identifies two main sources of pessimism of the initial RC method over best effort NoC. For each flow, constraints on the inter-release arrival of packets and the number of packets that can be emitted for a given interval are introduced to overcome them. However, these assumptions are at an application level, while we focus first on defining properties at the network level. Therefore, this is a complementary analysis that could be done after reducing the pessimism at the network level.

div.head: III. Problem statement and best-effort wormhole model
A. WCTT of flows
div.p: In this work, the problem we address is to compute upper-bounds on the WCTT of flows over best-effort NoCbased many-cores architectures. We assume that a set of tasks is statically allocated over a NoC and exchange various payloads. A payload is modeled as a flow and we note F the set of m flows of an application. Each flow f i (i = 1..m) is made of successive packets that are emitted between two tasks. Flows can have various requirements depending on whether it is a memory access, or inter-core communication of application-level data, an interrupt or an I/O access. For instance, memory accesses or interrupts have critical latency requirements and often a low payload, e.g. the size of a line of cache. Such flows are called latency-critical flows. Inter-core communications of application-level data can also be made of such type of latency-critical flows between sensors and actuators, as in classical safety-critical applications. Larger payloads can as well be exchanged between tasks, such as a streaming of MPEG data in less critical applications. However, the latency requirement of these flows is less strict than the one of latency-critical flows. In this work, we focus on such latency-critical flows.

div.head: B. System model
div.p: In this work, we model best-effort NoC-based manycores as a 2D-Mesh network with bidirectional links used to interconnect the m × m routers. Figure 1 illustrates a general NoC architecture. Except on the edge of the grid, each router has five input and five output ports fully interconnected. One pair of input and output is used to connect a core, while the other four remaining pairs connect to the other adjacent routers. Each input port consists of a single queuing buffer and thus do not support multiple VCs. The access to each output port, i.e. the link to an adjacent router, is arbitrated by a flow control policy. To ensure fairness between input ports, a RRA strategy is used to decide the next packet that will be sent. We therefore do not assume flit-level preemption. A roundrobin arbiter operates on the principle that a request which was served should have the lowest priority on the next round of arbitration [27]. These hypothesis correspond to what is commonly found in best-effort NoC-based manycore architectures, where each router has a very limited number of VCs [3] or even a single one [7], [29].

Packets of flows are transmitted over the NoC using the wormhole switching technique. Therefore, every packet is divided into a number of fixed size flits. The header flit governs the route. It indeed stores the routing information that is used at each router to select the output port. So, once the header flit arrives to the input port, it will be queued on the associated buffer. A credit-based mechanism controls the transmission rate of flits to routers. Once a flit is sent to the next router, the corresponding input port sends back a credit to the previous router allowing next flits to proceed. The remaining flits therefore follow in a pipeline way so forming a worm. When the header flit is blocked, then following flits may occupy several buffers at intermediate routers. This blocked message can therefore also block other messages. Thus, a flow cannot be analyzed independently from the other existing flows. We distinguish the flow to be analyzed from the other flows of F and we note it f a . The WCTT of f a depends on the resource contentions that f a encounters towards its destination. In fact, a flow can be classified as either being in direct or indirect contention with f a . A direct flow shares at least one link with f a , while an indirect flow shares at least one link only with a direct flow of f a . We also assume that packets are injected at a given inter-arrival time to prevent contentions with previous packets of the same flow to occur. Finally, we note that the destination router immediately consumes any flit arriving, as well as forwards back credit to the previous router.

div.head: C. Notations and definitions
div.p: At the hardware level, the switching delay of the header and the remaining flits are different. However, due to space constraints, in this paper, we assume that they are equals. Thus, we note d s the switching delay of a flit, i.e. the time required for the router to grant an output port for the packet. We note f size the size of a flit. The traversal delay of a link of capacity C, noted d t is thus equal to fsize C , should it be for regular data or credits due to the flow control. For the sake of readability, we assume in the remainder of this paper that d s = d t and we note
div.formula: d flit = d s + d t .
div.p: Let us assume in the remainder of the paper that d flit = 1 cycle. We also note by n fi the size of a packet of a flow f i in numbers of flits. We define F p ⊂ F the set of flows to be considered when analyzing f a , should they be in direct or indirect contention with f a . We also define F i,k the set of flows blocking f i on a router r k of its path. As explained in the previous section, due to the wormhole behavior F p = ∪ ∀r k ∈path(fa) F a,k , where path(f a ) returns the list of routers r k on the path of f a .

div.head: D. Problem illustration
div.p: Figure 2 shows the mapping of three flows (m = 3), noted f 1 , f 2 and f 3 , that is used in this section to illustrate the problem of computing upper-bounds of the WCTT. In this example, the analyzed flow f a is f 1 (f a = f 1 ). f 2 is in direct contention with f 1 , while f 3 in indirect contention with f 1 . Note that for the sake of readability, we have
div.formula: n f2 = n f1 = n f3 = 4.
div.p: In the recursive methods, f a is considered to be blocked till all the flows in contention arrive to their destinations. Its delay is therefore also made dependent on the remaining distance between its destination and the destination of the flows in contention. Also, these methods always consider the indirect flow as influent. We now show that this can be pessimistic, as also pointed out by [17]. For Fig. 3: Timeline of the transmission of flows f 1 , f 2 and f 3 . that, we use the timeline of the transmission of flits of flows from our example, that is shown in Figure 3. Each line represents a router, so once a flit is transmitted to the next router (i.e. lines between r k and r k+1 ), a credit is also transmitted to the previous router (i.e. lines between r k and r k-1 ). When the third flit of f 2 leaves r 2 at time t = 6, the header flit of f 1 is transmitted by r 1 . In this case, independently of the progression of f 2 towards its destination, in particular the blocking delay induced by f 3 over f 2 , f 2 will no longer impact the blocking delay of f 1 . It can also be noticed that f 3 does not block f 1 . The RC method computes 24.5 cycles for f 1 to reach its router of destination, while as seen on the timeline it takes 12.5 cycles.

By not considering the pipeline transmission, these methods lead to an over-approximation of WCTT. Thus, in our work, we have formulated properties to reduce this over-approximation. These properties are presented in the next section.

div.head: IV. Properties
div.p: In this section, we define three properties to be used when computing the WCTT of flows. The first one reduces the number of possible scenarios that must be explored by studying the arrivals of the flows on each router. The following ones concern the pipeline behavior of wormhole switching and its utilization for reducing the pessimism in the computation of WCTT.

div.head: A. Determination of worst-case scenarios
div.p: Computing a WCTT requires that the worst-case scenario has been identified. To identify such a worst-case scenario, the possible sequences of flows from F p over routers must be explored, even though all these scenarios do not lead to the WCTT. To reduce the number of scenarios to be explored when performing a WCTT analysis, we thus define a first property to focus on the worst-case scenario when computing the maximal blocking delay f a can suffer at each router. The first condition is obvious. Next, we have to prove that the condition of a synchronous arrival of headers leads to a worst case scenario.

Proof: let us assume that f a is blocked at router r k by two flows f i and f j . These flows have therefore in common a next router r k+1 in their paths towards their destinations. At least one link must indeed be shared between two flows so that they are in (direct) contention. When the headers of f a and f i arrive synchronously on r k , f a must wait till all the flits of f i leave r k+1 before being able to progress. This leads to a blocking delay D 1 equals to n fi ×2d flit , since the two routers r k and r k+1 must have transmitted all the flits of f i before being able to proceed another flow. Now, let us assume that n cfi flits of f i have already being transmitted by r k before the header of f a arrives at r k . Then, the blocking delay f a suffer before being able to progress is D 2 = (n fin cfi ) × 2d flit . As D 1 > D 2 , the synchronous arrival of headers is a worstcase scenario. the sake of readability, we assume all packets are made of 4 flits. We now focus of flows f 1 and f 2 only. Figure 5 presents a first scenario, noted (a), where f 1 and f 2 arrive synchronously at r 1 leading to D 1 = 4 × 2d flit . While in the second scenario also shown in Figure 5, noted (b), f 1 only waits D 2 = 2d flit as it arrives synchronously with the fourth and last flit of f 2 .

Finally, we have to prove the third condition of Property 1: the worst-case blocking delay of f a is obtained when f j arrives either synchronously with f a and f b or before the next round of arbitration.

Proof: if f j arrives after the current round of arbitration, it is clear that f a is going to progress before f j . In this case, the worst-case blocking delay that f a suffer (due to f b ) is equal to D 1 , previously introduced. Let us assume that f j arrives before the next round of arbitration and when n cf b flits of f b have been transmitted by r k . Meanwhile, f a was blocked for an amount of time equal to n cf b × 2d flit . However, the next round of arbitration only occurs when all flits of f b are transmitted by r k . The blocking delay that f a suffers is thus equal to n f b × 2d flit , independently of the number of flits that was transmitted before f j arrives. The next round of arbitration is won by f j due to the first condition of Property 1. Hence, f a is again blocked till all flits of f j are transmitted by r k . In total, f a thus is blocked for amount of time D 3 = (n f b + n fj ) × 2d flit . Now, let us assume that f j arrives before the synchronous arrival of f a and f b . f a is thus blocked for an amount of time equal to the remaining flits n cfj of f j to be transmitted when f a arrives at r k . The same rationale leads to a total worst-case blocking delay for f a equal to D 4 = (n f b + n cfj ) × 2d flit . As D 4 < D 3 , the worst-case blocking delay of f a is obtained when f j arrives either synchronously with f a and f b or before the next round of arbitration.

Note that if f j arrives synchronously with the arrival of f a and f b (i.e. n cf b = 0) the RRA and the first condition of Property 1 ensure that f a will be the last flow whose flits will be transmitted by r k . r k will either transmit f b Fig. 6: a scenario illustrating the third condition of Property 1. Fig. 7: timeline of the transmission of flows of the example shown in Figure 6. or f j first, however the blocking delay that f a will suffer is still equal to D 3 .

Figure 6 illustrates the third condition of Property 1 when the 3 flows of our example are considered. Here, we assume that f 1 and f 2 arrive synchronously, as previously, and that f 3 arrives with the fourth flit of f 2 . At this time, r 1 has transmitted three flits of f 2 . f 1 has thus been waiting for 3 × 2d flit and has to wait that r 1 transmits the last flit of f 2 . This total additional delay is thus equal to 4 × 2d flit . Then, f 1 will only be able to progress after all flits of f 3 have been transmitted by r 1 , since f 1 has arrived on the last port served by the RRA. This corresponds to an additional delay of 4 × 2d flit . Thus, the blocking delay f a suffer is equal to 8 × 2d flit . This delay is the same if f 3 arrives synchronously with f 1 and f 2 as shown in Figure 7.

We claim that the worst-case scenario is obtained when Property 1 is recursively applied to each flow that affects f a . This is illustrated in an example in Figure 8 where f 3 blocks f 2 and delays f 1 and f a = f 1 . As mentioned before, f 1 has to wait till the last common router between f 1 and f 2, i.e. r 3 , transmits all the flits of f 2 . However, f 2 will be blocked by f 3 at r 4 . Again, two scenarios can be defined at router r 4 , as shown in Figures 9a and9b. The scenario leading to the worst-case delay corresponds to Figure 9a. In this scenario, f 2 has indeed to wait that r 4 transmit all flits of f 3 before being able to progress. f 1 is thus blocked for a delay D 5 equals to (n f3 + n f2 ) × 2d flit before being able to progress. While, in the second scenario plotted in Figure 9b, n cf3 flits of f 3 have already been transmitted by r 4 before f 2 arrives at this router. f 1 thus waits a delay equals to (n f3n cf3 + n f2 ) × 2d flit , that is lower than D 5 . Fig. 8: example illustrating that Property 1 should be applied recursively.

div.head: B. Minimizing the pessimism in the computation of WCTT
div.p: To reduce the pessimism in the WCTT computation, two properties are defined. Note that Property 1 is applied when considering that a flow is being blocked by another one.

div.head: Property 2:
div.p: If f a is blocked by an unblocked flow f j , its maximal blocking delay is bounded by n fj × 2d flit .

As seen previously, if f a is blocked by f j at router r k , then these flows must have in common a next router r k+1 in their paths towards their destinations. At least one link must indeed be shared between two flows so that they are in (direct) contention. Due to the pipeline transmission, f a can progress only when the last flit of f j leaves their next common router r k+1 . f a is thus blocked for amount of time equals to 2n fj × d flit . Now, let us proof by contradiction that this delay t is the maximal blocking delay f a can suffer when it is blocked by an unblocked flow.

Proof: let us assume that a bigger blocking delay t 1 for f a exists. At time t 1 , f a should then still be blocked. At the same time, the header of f j should have been transmitted by router r k+2n f j and the (n fj -1) flits follow the header in a pipeline way. Thus, the last flit of f j is thus located within router r k+2 . f a has therefore progress at router r k+1 which is contradictory with the initial assumption. However, a flow f i could block f j at router r l . f j should be unblocked first, in order to unblock f a . This property must thus be applied recursively on all blocking flows. If r k = r l , the blocking delay of f j is equal also equals to t.

However, if r k = r l , f j can progress before being blocked. Once blocked, f j waits an amount of time equal to t to receive the credit from r l+1 . Meanwhile, f a is blocked at r k and waits for the credit from r k+1 to progress. This blocking delay depends on the number of hops, noted n hops , separating r k and r l . Three cases exists: 1) n hops = n fj . In this case, the last flit of f j is located within r k+1 when f j has reached r l , where it is blocked by f i . f a can thus immediately progress and its blocking delay D is thus equal to: n fj × d flit . 2) n hops > n fj . Compared to the previous case, some flits of f a must have already been transmitted by r k when f j reaches r l . The previous blocking delay of f a at r i is thus lowered by the number of routers the header of f a has crossed. This number is equal to n hopsn fj and the blocking delay to: D -(n hopsn fj ) × d flit . 3) n hops < n fj . In this case, a number of flits of f j must be located on r k and possibly on previous routers. f a is thus blocked till these flits of f j are transmitted by r k . This number is equal to n fjn hops . The blocking delay of f a of the first case therefore increases to:
In this last case, the blocking delay of f a is the higher one and is obviously lower than n fj × 2d flit .

We illustrate this property on the example of Figure 2. As shown in Figure 3, f 3 does not have an indirect influence on f 1 : f 1 is only blocked by f 2 . The maximal blocking delay of f 1 is thus equal to n f2 ×2d flit = 6 cycles.

Before presenting a third property, let us introduce some notations. We note f d a direct flow that blocks f a . The last common router between f a and f d is r k . We further assume that f d is also blocked by a flow f id at r l and is therefore an indirect flow of f a . We note E r the number of routers separating f a from f id . Property 3: if f a is blocked by f d which is also blocked by f id , then E r must be equal or higher than n f d -1 in order for f id to have no influence over f a .

Proof: if E r = n f d -1, the header of f d must therefore be blocked on r l . The remaining flits are thus located on routers r k+1 up to r l-1 . r k can therefore transmit the first flit of f a which will then be able to progress in a pipeline way. Consequently, f a is not affected by f id . If E r < n f d -1, a flit of f d must be located on r k since f d is blocked at r l by f id . f a is thus blocked on its path by f d and thus indirectly delay by f id .

In the example of Figure 2, f 3 does not affect f 1 if all packets are made of 3 flits. In this case, the header of f 2 is blocked at r 6 . The 2 nd and 3 rd flits are located at r 5 and r 4 . Hence, the path of f 1 is no more blocked. Now, let us consider packets of 4 flits. The 4 th flit of f 2 is then located at r 3 , blocking the progression of f 1 . So, f 3 indirectly affects f 1 .

div.head: C. Discussion
div.p: Let us stress that while examples assume that all packets have the same size, the properties we stated do not. Note that at the link level, transmission of flits cannot be pipelined as we assume within each router a buffer of one flit. However, this assumption ensure a worst-case Fig. 10: example illustrating the method of computation. scenario. Besides, if buffers of n b flits were assumed, we claim that these properties could be applied by considering each group of n b flits as equivalent to one flit, provided that n fi ≥ n b . We leave this generalization as future work.

div.head: V. Computing the WCTT
div.p: In this section, we will illustrate using an example our algorithm to compute WCTT of flows. We then describe how our algorithm implements the properties introduced at the previous section.

div.head: A. An example
div.p: We illustrate how our algorithm computes the WCTT of f 1 (f a = f 1 ) on the example shown in Figure 10. This example is made of 5 flows, where both f 2 and f 3 are in direct contention with f 1 . Both f 4 and f 5 are in indirect contention with f 1 as they are in direct contention with f 2 and share no common routers with f 1 .

First, we have to build for each flow the list of flows in direct contention. We note L fi the list of such blocking flows of f i which is made of a set of couples < f j , r k > where f j is a flow in direct contention with f i . r k is the first common router between f i and f j . The flows are ordered by the round robin arbitration, assuming Property 1. To identify when f i can be transmitted by r k and then progress, i.e. it is no longer blocked, f i is also added in L fi . For instance, in our example,

div.p: Then, when stepping through the L fi lists, it can be noticed that f 2 is blocked by f 4 and f 5 . Since both f 4 and f 5 are indirect flows of f 3 and f 1 , two scenarios can occur:

• If n f2 = 2, Property 3 applies and f 4 has no indirect influence over f 3 . Consequently, f 2 becomes an unblocked flow for f 3 , allowing to apply Property 2 to compute the maximal blocking delay of f 3 . Since in turn f 3 becomes an unblocked flow for f 1 , property 2 also applies for computing the blocking delay of f 1 . Then the transmission time of f 1 till its destination must be added to compute its WCTT. • If n f2 > 2, f 4 can have an influence over f 3 but has an influence over f 1 . Let us assume that f 4 has an influence on both of these flows and therefore must be analyzed. L f4 tells us that it is blocked by f 5 , also requiring the analysis of f 5 in order to compute the WCTT of f 1 .
This behavior has been implemented into an algorithm that is described in the next section.

div.head: B. Description of the algorithm
div.p: Our algorithm is divided into two parts. The goal of the first part is to identify all the blocking flows of f a , i.e. to compute F p . Each flow of L fa are added in F p , using Property 1. As seen previously, it is also necessary to f.setT o(f.f bnext ) 20:

This recursion ends when no new flows are added to F p . Some particular cases are considered such the RRA to choose one blocking flow from each port and when f a is blocked at the source node by another flow.

Then, Algorithm 1 illustrates the second part of our algorithm. It computes the WCTT of f a by adding each time the necessary delay so that flows that interfere with f a can progress and therefore unblock f a . Therefore, for each analyzed flow f , we compute (lines 3 to 6): its first direct blocking flow in L f (noted f b ), its next direct blocking flow in L f (f bnext ), the blocking flow of f b in L f b (f bb ) its next blocking flow in L f b (f bbnext ). In the case where f b is no longer blocked, f bb = f b by definition on how lists of blocking flows are built. f b can therefore progress to give the credit to f bnext at router r bnext , which corresponds to the use of the Property 2 to compute the delay. If a flow blocked by f exists, its analyze started in a previous iteration must next be resumed (not shown due to space constraint). When f b is blocked by f bb , f bb can be either in direct or indirect contention with flow f bnext . If f bb is in direct contention, the time needed by f b to progress to r bb its bocking router must first be accounted (line 11). div.head: VI. Applications and Results
div.p: This section presents an evaluation of our algorithm made over two applications and compared to the RC method [9], as this method matches our hypothesis. Besides, we compare ourself to the RC method because we focus on the improvements provided by properties stated at the network level only. To quantify the improvements, we compute the following metric: (dRC -dA)×100

div.head: d.RC
div.p: , where d RC is the WCTT value returned by the RC method and d A the value returned by our algorithm. We also report on the modifications of some parameters, such as the number of flits or the size of the NoC, affect our results.

No standard real-time benchmarks exist for manycores. We therefore used a SpaceWire application and an application implementing a Fast-Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. Since NoCs used within many-cores are larger than a SpaceWire network, we vary the destination of flows of the initial SpaceWire application. As a first step of our analysis, we drive our study on latency critical messages where we consider 19 flits as the maximum size of packets [28]. We further assume that n fi are equals.

div.head: A. Synthetic benchmark
div.p: We consider the mapping shown in Figure 11a, extracted from a SpaceWire application [9]. We compute the WCTT of f 1 , i.e. f a = f 1 , and present several configurations to explain the gain due to the Properties 2 and 3. a) First configuration: its goal is to quantify, over specific mapping of flows over a NoC, how the Property 2 improves WCTT. As shown in Figure 11a, we generate different mapping of flows by modifying the destination of some of the direct flows represented in dotted lines. For each mapping, we compute the WCTT in order to study how the number of hops, they make after the destination of f 1 , affects the results. For instance, a number of hops equals to 0 means that these direct flows have the same destination as f 1 . Figure 11b shows the gain obtained for various number of hops. While in the RC method, a flow cannot progress until its direct blocking (but unblocked) flow reaches its destination, Property 2 states that this delay only depends on the number of flits of the direct flow. For packets of a given number of flits, the WCTT computed by RC therefore increases with the number of hops, while it is constant using our algorithm. The blocked flow indeed always waits for the same amount of time the credit from the blocking direct flow, independently of its destination, explaining the shape of the curve. For a given number of hops, the gain decreases with the increase in the number of flits making a packet. The blocking delay in both methods indeed increases as more flits of the direct blocking flows have to be transmitted by routers. b) Second configuration: its goal is to quantify the gain, over specific mapping of flows, due to Property 3. Compared to the previous configuration, we therefore add an indirect flow f 7 , that blocks f 5 a direct flow of f 1 , as shown in Figure 12a. We also set the destination of f 5 21 hops after the destination of f 1 . The value of E r is one parameter that determines whether an indirect flow is influent or not, the router where f 7 blocks f 5 ranges from r 5 to r 23 . Figure 12b shows the gain for various values of E r and for different length of packets. For a given length of packets, the two constant obtained gains are explained by the 21 hops that f 5 performs to reach its destination which are accounted in the WCTT computed by the RC method. The existence of the two constants gains comes from whether Property 3 applies or not. When E r < n fi (left part of the curves), f 7 indirectly blocks f 1 and thus influences its WCTT. However, when E r ≥ n fi the RC method still assumes that f 7 influences f 1 and thus adds it in the computation of the WCTT of f 1 . Our algorithm instead identifies that f 7 is not influent as Property 3 applies. This difference leads to an increase in the obtained gain and the second plateau in the curves shown in Figure 12b.

div.head: B. Fast-Fourier Transform (FFT)
div.p: Then, we evaluate whether the properties implemented by our algorithm apply in a widespread algorithm used within signal processing and embedded control applications: the FTT algorithm [8]. We focus on the communication patterns exhibited by two stages of a classical FFT algorithm, since they lead to contentions between flows. In stage 2, whose mapping is shown in Figure 13a on a subset of a 6×6 NoC (first row only), each core exchanges data with another one and performs some local computation. In stage 5, whose mapping is shown over a 4×4 NoC in Figure 13b, data computed by each core are gathered by specific core. Similarly to the previous section, we compute the WCTT of f 1 for various size of the NoC and number of flits making packets. Note that when the size of the NoC is increased, we add a number of flows to preserve the existing communication pattern. c) Stage 2: for a given size of packets and as shown in Figure 14, the gain increases with the size of NoC as more hops are performed by the additional direct flows. It is the Property 2 that improves the computed WCTT, the mapping of flows of stage 2 exhibiting similar contentions as in the first configuration of the SpaceWire application. The same conclusion thus applies.

d) Stage 5: we obtain a gain of 11.38% in the computed WCTT for packets made of 2 flits and a gain of 1.27% for packets made of 19 flits. For a given size of packets, the gain remains approximately constant with the size of the NoC increases. Property 2 states that a flow only has to wait that its blocking flow releases their last common router. This property thus provides an important gain, compared to the RC method, only when the blocking flow is not blocked. In stage 5, each flow is however blocked at each router until it reaches r 16 , the destination common to all flows. Thus, the gain only slowly increases.

div.head: C. Discussion
div.p: Considering the pipeline transmission of flits in the WCTT computation reduces the pessimism introduced by the recursive methods. This improvement depends on the type of contentions, the size of the NoC and the size of packets. The Property 2 improves WCTT values when the size of NoC is large and the size of packets small or when the number of hops performed by flows is greater than the size of packets in flits. The Property 3 helps when the size of NoC is sufficient for indirect contentions to occur with a minimum spacing between analyzed flows and indirect ones.

div.head: VII. Conclusion and future work
div.p: The RC method [9], used for computing the WCTT in wormhole networks, considers that an analyzed flow can be blocked by others flows while these last flows have not reach their destinations. RC thus adds the transmission delays of the blocking flows to the WCTT analyzed flow, leading to an over-approximation. However, we have shown that the pipeline transmission of flits over NoC can be used to reduce the maximal blocking delay an analyzed flow can suffer due to these blocking flows, thus tightening computed WCTTs. Thus, we introduce three properties to either reduce the number of scenarios to be explored when performing a WCTT analysis or the computed WCTTs. The first property states the worst-case scenario when computing the maximal blocking delay a flow can suffer when a roundrobin arbiter is used. The second property states that the maximal blocking delay a flow can suffer due to an unblock is bounded by the number of flits of the unblock flow, thus eliminating the need to wait till the unblocked flow reaches its destination. A third property allows to check whether an indirect flow influences the transmission delay of an analyzed flow. These properties are used in the algorithm we present in this paper to improves the WCTT as shown in the evaluation we report. We compare our method to RC only as we focus on properties at the network level. [6] is thus complementary to our work and could be used to further reduce the pessimism of computed WCTTs. Furthermore, we show how some parameters affect the gain we obtained related to RC thanks to use of these properties.

As further work, we plan to study WCTT when assuming buffers within routers have a capacity of more than one flit. We also plan to consider the support of multiple VCs and evaluate our algorithm with packets of different sizes.
